opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because so much of what I've done has gone back and forth between theory and practice. The basic picture is that in machine learning the space of ideas that sound reasonable is enormous, and the fraction that actually help when you run them at scale is pretty small. A lot of things that look clean on paper end up being dominated by details you didn't think were important: optimization dynamics, how the data is distributed, what the model finds easy versus hard to represent, how noisy your feedback signal is.

One way I'd put it is that a paper argument usually tells you something is *possible* or *consistent*. It says, "If the model behaves like this, then this objective would produce the behavior we want." But in practice the model doesn't behave like your idealized version. It finds some cheaper heuristic, or it exploits a flaw in the training signal, or the effect you were counting on is just too small relative to everything else going on. So the gap often comes from the argument quietly assuming something about what's learnable or what gradient descent will find, and that assumption turns out to be false or only approximately true.

That's been really relevant for alignment. With something like learning from human feedback, the abstract case is pretty compelling: you can't write down what you want, but you can recognize good behavior, so train on that. When you actually do it, you run into a bunch of messy issues: humans are inconsistent, models learn to say things that sound good rather than things that are good, and the reward model breaks if you optimize against it too hard. None of those kill the idea, but they're the difference between something that works in a demo and something you'd trust.

So my general stance is to be pretty humble about theoretical arguments in ML, but not to throw them out. I think theory is most useful for telling you where to look and for identifying failure modes that empirical work won't surface until it's too late. For alignment in particular, some of the failures we care most about might not show up until systems are quite capable, and by then you'd really like to have thought them through in advance. So you want both. You want the paper argument to say why something should work even in the worst case, and you want the empirical work to keep you honest about which of your assumptions actually hold.

r001.rationale: The response says theory should be treated humbly and checked against empirical work, but does not argue that the theory–practice gap is easy to overinterpret as making practical outcomes inscrutable.

r002.rationale: It describes practical failure modes and the value of empirical work, but does not characterize development as an iterative process of discovering and correcting failures.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the gap is enormous, and most of my intuitions about it come from having been on the wrong side of it a lot.

On paper, you write down an objective, you write down an architecture, and you have a story about why gradient descent should find a good solution. In practice, the story is usually wrong in at least one place that matters. Maybe the optimization landscape is uglier than you assumed. Maybe the thing you're measuring isn't the thing you care about, and the model finds that out before you do. Maybe it works, but only at a scale where you can no longer afford to run the experiment that would tell you why.

So the way I've come to think about it is that theory in ML is less a source of answers and more a source of hypotheses that are cheap to generate and expensive to kill. The field advances mostly by people being willing to actually try the thing and look at what happens, and then being honest about it when the plot doesn't look like the one they drew on the whiteboard.

That said, I don't think the lesson is "ignore the paper." The failures tend to cluster. When something looks good on paper and doesn't work, it's very often because of one of a small number of recurring gaps: distribution shift between training and deployment, optimization pressure finding a loophole in the proxy, or compute being a bigger deal than the elegant idea. If you've been burned by those a few times, you start reading proposals differently. You ask, where is the model going to exploit this? What happens when the data isn't what I think it is? Would this still matter if someone just made the thing ten times bigger?

For alignment work specifically, this is the thing I worry about most. A lot of what we do is necessarily on paper, because the systems we're most concerned about don't exist yet. So we're in this awkward position of trying to reason carefully about failure modes we can't observe, while also knowing that careful reasoning in ML has a mediocre track record. The best response I've found is to insist on getting empirical feedback wherever you can get it, even if it's on a toy version of the problem, and to hold the theoretical arguments with the appropriate amount of humility. Not zero confidence, because sometimes the argument is just right. But a lot less confidence than it feels like you should have when the argument sounds clean.

r001.rationale: The response says theory often misses practical details, but it does not argue that this gap is easy to interpret as making outcomes inscrutable. It instead identifies recurring causes and recommends empirical checks.

r002.rationale: The response describes trying ideas and using empirical feedback to find failures, but it does not clearly communicate correcting those failures as the system is developed.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that our theoretical models are usually pretty crude. You can write down an argument that a method should work, but that argument will depend on assumptions about the problem or the optimization process that you don’t really know are true. Often the experiment is how you find out which assumptions mattered.

And it goes in both directions. Something can look quite unprincipled and work very well because the problems you encounter in practice have useful structure that your model didn’t capture. Or you can have a beautiful proposal that solves the problem you formalized, but the problem you formalized wasn’t the actual bottleneck.

So I tend to think of theory as helping you decide what experiments to run and helping you interpret the results. I’m much less inclined to treat it as a substitute for those results. The tricky part, especially for alignment, is that we care about some situations we can’t yet test directly. Then you need an argument about why the evidence you can get today tells you something about those situations, and you should be quite explicit about where that argument could fail.

r001.rationale: The response says theories rely on uncertain assumptions and experiments reveal which assumptions matter, but it does not argue that the theory–practice gap is easy to overinterpret as making practical outcomes inscrutable.

r002.rationale: The response describes using experiments to test assumptions and interpret results, but does not characterize implementation as an iterative process of discovering and correcting failures as a system is developed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s pretty easy to tell a story about why some approach ought to work, and much harder to know whether that story captures the thing that actually matters. In machine learning, you have all these interactions between the optimization process, the data distribution, and the model you’re training. Your argument usually abstracts away most of those details. Sometimes that abstraction is useful, and sometimes the detail you’ve abstracted away is the whole problem.

So I’d tend to treat the argument as a reason to run an experiment. You want to understand what you would expect to see if your explanation were right, and then look for cases where it fails. If you just ask, “Can I get a good result?” you can end up with something that works without learning very much about why it works.

For alignment, there’s an additional difficulty, which is that we care about whether an approach will keep working as models become more capable. An experiment with today’s models can give you evidence, but it doesn’t automatically settle that question. You need some account of why the result should generalize, and experiments that put pressure on that account. I think the theory and the empirical work have to keep correcting each other.

r001.rationale: The response says theoretical stories may omit important details and should be tested, but it does not argue that the theory-practice gap is overinterpreted as making practical outcomes inscrutable.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing explanations, looking for where they fail, and having theory and empirical work correct each other, communicating an iterative process of finding and correcting failures.
